B07_00: HGF-activated MET controls epithelial scattering, wound closure and invasive growth, and its coupling to tensins at focal adhesions links this signal to substrate grip. MET associates with reciprocally expressed tensins: TNS4 stabilises the receptor and favours motility, while TNS3 predominates in less migratory states. Because tensins bridge beta-1 integrin to actin, growth factor signalling reaches adhesion machinery, and elevated TNS4 accompanies MET-driven carcinoma invasion.
B07_01: Neuropilins are kinase-less co-receptors that bind selected VEGF ligands and present them to VEGF receptors, tuning endothelial responses in blood and lymphatic vessel growth. NRP1 binds VEGF-A165, VEGF-B and PlGF-2, while NRP2 also binds VEGF-A145 and VEGF-C, and both pair with KDR or FLT1 to raise ligand affinity. NRP1 favours arterial and NRP2 venous and lymphatic vessels; the interface is targeted in tumour angiogenesis.
B07_02: One branch of EGF receptor signalling runs through phospholipid turnover. Ligands such as EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin and HB-EGF activate the receptor, which recruits PLCG1 via its SH2 domains; phosphorylated PLCG1 cleaves PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol, releasing stored calcium and activating protein kinase C. These signals drive epithelial proliferation, migration and cytoskeletal remodelling, and contribute to growth and invasion of EGFR-driven carcinomas.
B07_03: This VEGFR2 branch drives endothelial proliferation, underlying angiogenesis in development, wound healing and tumours and targeted by anti-VEGF drugs. VEGFA binding to KDR triggers Src-dependent phosphorylation that activates PLC gamma, whose IP3 releases ER calcium that, with calmodulin and diacylglycerol, activates PKC. PKC feeds the Ras-Raf-MEK-ERK cascade via Raf phosphorylation or relief of Ras GAP restraint, with sphingosine kinase and PDPK1 adding survival input.
B07_04: The PI3K-AKT branch of HGF-MET signalling supports epithelial survival, motility and regeneration in liver, kidney and skin, and helps MET-driven tumours resist apoptosis and invade. Activated MET recruits GRB2 and GAB1, then phosphorylates GAB1 to dock PIK3R1, and PIK3CA generates PIP3 to activate AKT, suppressing apoptosis and promoting mTOR-dependent growth. MET amplification, mutation or stromal HGF sustains this signal, targeted by MET kinase inhibitors.
B07_05: ERBB4 can signal in the nucleus: neuregulin binding to JM-A isoforms triggers ADAM17 shedding and gamma-secretase cleavage, releasing a soluble intracellular domain that acts as a transcriptional co-factor. With TAB2 and NCOR1 it represses astrocytic genes in neural precursors, with STAT5A drives beta-casein during lactation, and with estrogen receptor induces progesterone receptor and CXCL12. YAP1 and WWOX govern nuclear entry, linking this to mammary differentiation and breast cancer.
B07_06: ERBB4 signalling is terminated by ubiquitin-dependent destruction of the receptor and its cleavage fragments, setting how much neuregulin input drives proliferation, differentiation or nuclear regulation in heart, nervous system and tumours. WW-domain motifs recruit the NEDD4-family ligases WWP1, ITCH and NEDD4, which ubiquitinate intact ERBB4 and its fragments for proteasomal and lysosomal degradation, limiting nuclear entry. Binding is activation-independent and modulated by SRC phosphorylation.
B07_07: This canonical step converts ligand-activated EGF receptor into active RAS. Ligands including EGF, TGF-alpha, amphiregulin and HB-EGF dimerise the receptor and trigger tail phosphorylation; GRB2 docks via its SH2 domain while holding SOS1, delivering it to the membrane to load GTP onto HRAS, KRAS and NRAS. Output feeds the MAP kinase cascade for growth and survival, and activating EGFR or RAS mutations drive lung and colorectal carcinomas.
B07_08: ERBB2 heterodimers with EGFR, ERBB3 or ERBB4 also direct cell migration, important in wound closure and morphogenesis and in invasion of ERBB2-amplified breast cancer. Ligands such as EGF, betacellulin, heregulins and HB-EGF trigger receptor phosphorylation that docks MEMO1. MEMO1 holds active RHOA and the formin DIAPH1 at the membrane, coordinating actin polymerisation and microtubule capture for directed lamellipodial protrusion and stable polarity.
B07_09: Vessel growth begins when VEGF ligands bind and dimerise VEGF receptors, initiating endothelial proliferation, survival, migration and permeability, the step tumours use to recruit blood supply and anti-angiogenic drugs target. VEGFA, VEGFB, PlGF, VEGFC and VEGFD bind FLT1, KDR and FLT4 with distinct preferences, mostly as homodimers. KDR carries most angiogenic signalling, FLT1 acts as a decoy, and FLT4 specifies lymphatics; dysregulation causes malformations, lymphoedema and pathological neovascularisation.
B07_10: One branch of ERBB4 signalling recruits PI3K, supporting survival, migration and differentiation in nervous system, heart and mammary epithelium; disruption is linked to cardiomyopathy and schizophrenia risk. Neuregulins and EGF-family ligands drive receptor dimerisation and autophosphorylation. Only CYT1 splice isoforms retain the tyrosine that docks p85 alpha, recruiting p110 alpha to generate PIP3 and activate AKT, so splicing determines whether ERBB4 couples to survival signalling.
B07_11: MET activation involves proteolytic maturation of HGF and ligand-driven MET dimerisation, producing signals for epithelial survival, scattering, motility and branching that underpin liver and placental development and tissue repair. Inert single-chain HGF is cleaved by hepsin or HGFAC, proteases restrained by SPINT1 and SPINT2. Mature HGF binds the MET SEMA and PSI domains, promoting pairing and trans-autophosphorylation; excessive MET activation drives invasive carcinoma.
B07_12: HGF-MET drives cell movement through focal adhesion kinase, which is activated only when engaged simultaneously by MET and matrix-bound integrins, with SRC phosphorylation needed for full activity. Fibronectin, collagens and laminins supply the matrix side through beta1-containing integrins. The output is adhesion turnover and directed migration in wound epithelialisation and branching morphogenesis, and invasion and metastasis when MET is amplified or stromal HGF is present.
B07_13: After HGF binding, MET is internalised, and its endosomal route determines signal duration and strength. Recycling to the membrane sustains ERK and STAT3 output supporting motility, scattering and invasive growth, also exploited in carcinoma. GGA3 sorts MET through RAB4-marked recycling endosomes with ARF6 aiding return, while GRB2, GAB1, CRK and CRKL stay bound and signal from endosomes; diversion to degradation shortens the response.
B07_14: In one branch of HGF-MET signalling, STAT3 docks at a phosphorylated MET tail tyrosine, directly or via a scaffold, and is phosphorylated on Y705, enabling dimerisation, nuclear entry and target gene expression; SRC and endosomal signalling contribute. The output is anchorage-independent proliferation and motility, relevant in carcinomas with MET amplification or autocrine HGF. Normally the route supports epithelial repair, liver regeneration and branching morphogenesis.
B07_15: This negative feedback limits ERBB2:ERBB3 signalling by controlling surface ERBB3. Neuregulin activates AKT, which phosphorylates and stabilises the deubiquitinase USP8, preventing RNF41 self-ubiquitination; stabilised RNF41 then ubiquitinates ERBB3 for degradation. Low RNF41 lets ERBB3 persist and raises neuregulin sensitivity, and loss of this brake sustains PI3K-AKT signalling and resistance to ERBB2-directed therapy in breast and epithelial cancers.
B07_16: Ligand-activated EGFR is removed from the cell surface and destroyed to limit signalling, and loss of this brake promotes epithelial tumours. After autophosphorylation, the ubiquitin ligase CBL is recruited directly and via GRB2 to ubiquitinate the receptor; CIN85 links CBL to endophilins for clathrin-coated pit formation, while EPS15, epsin and HGS/STAM sort cargo into multivesicular bodies for lysosomal degradation. PTPN12 and Sprouty proteins add negative feedback.
B07_17: The PLCG1 arm of ERBB2 signalling steers cells toward motility and calcium-dependent responses. Ligand-bound EGFR heterodimerises with ERBB2, and PLCG1 docks on tail phosphotyrosines such as EGFR Y992 and Y1173, hydrolysing PIP2 into IP3 and diacylglycerol to release stored calcium and activate PKC. This drives actin remodelling, migration and secretion and contributes to invasive ERBB2-amplified breast tumours, showing how partner choice shapes second messengers.
B07_18: HGF-MET signalling drives epithelial cell movement by activating RAP1 and RAC1, promoting scattering, lamellipodia, spreading and integrin adhesion in wound healing, liver regeneration and morphogenesis, and in carcinoma invasion. Activated MET recruits GRB2 and GAB1, whose phosphotyrosines bind CRK and CRKL. These dock RAPGEF1, which activates RAP1A and RAP1B to strengthen adhesion, and DOCK7, which activates RAC1 for leading-edge actin polymerisation.
B07_19: Much HGF-MET output for epithelial proliferation, survival, scattering and morphogenesis runs through RAS and sustained ERK activity. MET phosphotyrosines recruit GRB2 and SHC1 or scaffolds such as RANBP9, which bring SOS1 to load GTP onto HRAS, KRAS and NRAS. Signalling continues from endosomes, MUC20 and RANBP10 dampen it, and constitutive activity through MET amplification or mutation sustains invasive carcinoma growth targeted by kinase inhibitors.
B07_20: ERBB2 (HER2) amplification drives aggressive breast and gastric cancers, and blocking it is a major targeted therapy success. Kinase inhibitors such as lapatinib, neratinib and afatinib occupy the ATP site, while antibodies such as trastuzumab and pertuzumab bind the ectodomain to block dimerisation and promote downregulation, removing PI3K-AKT and MAPK input. HSP90 with CDC37 stabilises ERBB2, ERBIN restrains it, and resistance arises through mutation or bypass receptors.
B07_21: HGF-activated MET drives scattering, motility, invasion and survival, and becomes oncogenic when amplified or mutated; it also emerges as an escape route in tumours treated against EGFR. MET is drugged by monoclonal antibodies that intercept HGF or block ligand-induced receptor dimerisation, and by small-molecule kinase inhibitors that block catalytic activity. Both abolish MET autophosphorylation and adaptor recruitment that would feed proliferative and invasive signalling in MET-driven solid tumours.
B07_22: Neuregulins and EGF-family ligands activate ERBB4, and one main output runs through the adaptor SHC1 to RAS-MAPK signalling, supporting proliferation and differentiation in neural, cardiac and mammary tissue; disturbance is linked to schizophrenia and breast cancer. Autophosphorylated ERBB4 tail tyrosines dock SHC1 via its PTB domain, ERBB4 phosphorylates SHC1, and GRB2 brings SOS1 to load GTP onto RAS, engaging RAF-MEK-ERK.
B07_23: After insulin-receptor internalisation, recycling destroys insulin and returns the receptor to the surface, setting how long cells stay insulin-responsive and how fast insulin is cleared, relevant to type 2 diabetes. The vacuolar ATPase acidifies endosomes, releasing insulin for degradation by insulin-degrading enzyme and cathepsin D. Phosphatases PTP1B and PTPRF dephosphorylate the receptor kinase, ending signalling and restoring a ligand-free receptor to the membrane.
B07_24: When ERBB2 heterodimerises with EGFR or ERBB4, tail phosphotyrosines dock GRB2, converting EGF-family or neuregulin binding into RAS-dependent proliferation. GRB2-bound SOS1 loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS, activating RAF and the MAPK cascade for cell cycle entry, growth and survival in epithelial, cardiac, neural and repair contexts. ERBB2 amplification in breast and gastric cancer drives constitutive output through this step, and downstream RAS mutation confers resistance.
B07_25: The adaptor SHC1 provides one of two routes from ligand-bound EGFR to RAS. SHC1 docks on phosphorylated receptor tails via SH2 and PTB domains, becomes phosphorylated and recruits GRB2-SOS1, which loads GTP onto HRAS, KRAS or NRAS to drive MAPK-dependent proliferation, survival and migration. Any EGFR ligand, many proteolytically shed, can trigger it, and activating EGFR or RAS mutations drive lung, colorectal and head and neck cancers.
B07_26: The non-receptor kinase PTK6 (BRK) is activated downstream of ERBB2, linking growth factor signalling to epithelial proliferation, migration and survival; in breast cancer it co-occurs with ERBB2 amplification and supports therapy resistance. EGF-family ligands and neuregulins drive dimerisation with ERBB2 as preferred partner coupling complexes to PTK6, and EGFR or MET signals may be relayed via ERBB2. PTK6 then phosphorylates cytoskeletal, STAT and anti-apoptotic substrates.
B07_27: When neuregulin drives ERBB2-ERBB3 heterodimers, ERBB3 tail phosphotyrosines recruit the non-catalytic adaptor GRB7. Via SHC1 it contributes to RAS activation and growth, and when phosphorylated by integrin-activated FAK it promotes VAV2-dependent RAC1 activation and motility, though mechanisms remain incompletely defined. GRB7 is co-amplified with neighbouring ERBB2 on chromosome 17 in breast cancer, coupling receptor overexpression to invasion and proliferation.
B07_28: ERBB2 signalling converges on SHC1 to activate RAS and the RAF-MAPK cascade, driving proliferation and survival in epithelial, cardiac and neural tissue and acting as a major oncogenic output in ERBB2-amplified breast and gastric cancer. Ligandless ERBB2 partners EGFR, ERBB3 and ERBB4 bound by EGF-family or neuregulin ligands. SHC1 docks on phosphorylated tails and recruits GRB2-SOS1 to activate RAS, while PKC isoforms and PTPN12 tune output.
B07_29: VEGFR2 signalling makes vessels dilate and leak, enabling plasma extravasation for sprouting angiogenesis and causing oedema in tumours, diabetic retinopathy and inflammation. AKT, activated with PDPK1 and mTORC2 components, phosphorylates eNOS, which with calmodulin, HSP90 and caveolin-1 releases nitric oxide to relax smooth muscle. In parallel, VAV-RAC1-PAK signalling triggers VE-cadherin endocytosis, dismantling adherens junctions with their catenin partners.
B07_30: Insulin signal attenuation returns cells to baseline after an insulin pulse. After insulin dissociates and is degraded in endosomes, endosome-associated tyrosine phosphatases dephosphorylate the insulin receptor and IRS1 and IRS2, releasing GRB2, SHC1 and SOS1 so ERK-activating complexes disassemble, while GRB10 adds negative regulation. Failed shutdown leaves growth and metabolic signalling running, whereas excessive attenuation contributes to insulin resistance.
B07_31: ERBB2-containing heterodimers promote survival, growth and metabolism via PI3K-AKT, and ERBB2 amplification with PIK3CA mutations in breast and gastric cancer creates dependence on this arm and shapes HER2 therapy response. Neuregulins binding ERBB3 or ERBB4, or EGF-family ligands binding EGFR, drive heterodimerisation with ERBB2. p85 docks directly on ERBB3 or ERBB4 CYT1 tails, or via GRB2-GAB1 with EGFR, recruiting p110 to make PIP3 and activate AKT.
B07_32: Activated EGFR reaches the AKT survival and growth arm through the GAB1 signalosome. EGFR ligands activate the receptor, which binds GRB2 and the scaffold GAB1, recruiting PIK3R1 and PIK3CA to convert PIP2 to PIP3 and trigger AKT-dependent proliferation and apoptosis resistance. GAB1 also docks PTPN11 and links to SRC kinases restrained by CSK and PAG1, with paxillin tying in adhesion; excess flux is common in EGFR-driven cancers.
B07_33: HGF-MET drives epithelial scattering, motility, repair and morphogenesis and is hijacked in carcinomas, with one branch running through the phosphatase PTPN11 (SHP2). Activated MET recruits GRB2 and GAB1, which docks PTPN11 for HGF-induced phosphorylation. PTPN11 sustains ERK1/2 activation and sphingosine kinase activation, linking to lipid messengers and scattering, while also dephosphorylating MET, so this arm both propagates and limits signalling.
B07_34: IRS activation couples insulin binding to PI3K-dependent glucose uptake and glycogen synthesis and to Ras-MAPK growth signalling. The activated insulin receptor recruits IRS1 or IRS2 via the PTB domain, with the PH domain anchoring membranes, and phosphorylates multiple tyrosines so SH2 partners can bind; GRB10 competes and dampens output. Loss or serine-phosphorylation-driven inactivation of IRS proteins underlies insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes.
